question: In 2019, the YouTube science series “Because Science” had Olympic sprinter Jeneba Tarmoh try this running style over a 50-meter dash. The experiment clocked it about three percent slower than her ordinary sprint, largely because it removes a runner’s arm counterbalance. The pose actually predates the anime that popularized it, having already been used to depict sprinting ninja in Japanese films and television of the 1960s and 70s. It became a nationwide talking point in the United States in September 2019, after thousands of people “signed up” online to raid a secretive Nevada Air Force base. Many of them joked that they would cross its perimeter using exactly this running style. Practitioners lean their torso forward and swing both arms straight out behind them at hip height instead of pumping them normally. For 10 points, name this sprinting style named for a spiky-haired, orange-jumpsuited ninja protagonist.

Attached to “nin,” this word names the historical ninja arts of stealth, infiltration and combat. Attached to “tai” instead, it names an unarmed martial art built on body movement rather than throws or strikes. In the ninja anime “Naruto,” sword-fighting’s “kenjutsu” and the illusion-casting “genjutsu” — a signature ability of one clan of antagonists — both end in this word too. That same anime conventionally names its techniques with this word attached. Its blond ninja hero shouts the name of his signature shadow-clone technique before a puff of smoke reveals dozens of copies of himself. Fans have jokingly appended “Talk no” to this word to describe that hero’s habit of ending fights with a heartfelt speech instead of violence. For 10 points, give this Japanese word for “technique” or “art,” also combined with “ju” to name a grappling martial art and its anime-fueled modern cousin.

This character’s iconic hat was given to him at age seven by Red-Haired Shanks, a former crewmate of the pirate king Gol D. Roger. Shanks told him to return the hat once he became a great pirate. Guinness World Records recognized “One Piece,” the manga starring this character, for surpassing 500 million copies printed by a single author as of 2022. In a 2023 anime episode whose wild, cartoonish art style fans both praised and mocked, this character unlocks “Gear Fifth” by awakening his Devil Fruit’s true form. That form is the mythical “Sun God Nika”. As a child, he unknowingly ate the Gum-Gum Fruit, which turned his body to rubber. For 10 points, name this rubber-limbed pirate captain, who leads the Straw Hat Pirates in a quest to become the Pirate King, and who is nicknamed for his straw hat.

A 2011 physics paper modeling cultural spread used this word and its Kansai-region rival “aho” as a case study, since the two insults radiate outward from Kyoto in concentric rings. That pattern echoes folklorist Kunio Yanagita’s 1930 “concentric circle theory” of Japanese dialect distribution, which places older word forms farthest from Kyoto. In the 1980s, English-speaking fans of the anime “Urusei Yatsura” began pairing a character’s name with this word as an injoke. They had borrowed the phrase from alien schoolgirl Lum, who would shout it at her boyfriend before shocking him with lightning. A 2010 school comedy anime takes its English title from this word paired with “and Test,” set among students whose exam scores summon battle avatars. Typically translated as “idiot” or “fool,” this word is a mainstay insult shouted by tsundere anime characters at their crush. For 10 points, give this common Japanese put-down.

Voice actress Saki Fujita recorded the vocal samples used to build this character’s software voicebank for Yamaha’s Vocaloid2 engine, released by Crypton Future Media on August 31, 2007. Illustrator KEI, who has said he did not know what a synthesizer was beforehand, designed this character’s turquoise twin-tails and schoolgirl outfit around Yamaha’s signature blue-green color scheme. Fans created a chibi, doll-eyed spinoff of this character after she appeared shaking a leek in a 2007 music video for a cover of the Finnish folk song “Ievan Polkka”. That leek-spinning meme had actually begun the previous year with an unrelated anime clip. In 2014, she appeared as a 3D hologram opening act on more than a dozen North American stops of Lady Gaga’s “ArtRave: The Artpop Ball” tour. Her name combines Japanese words for “first,” “sound” and “future”. For 10 points, name this turquoise-haired virtual idol, the flagship character of the Vocaloid singing-synthesizer software.

This franchise’s first giant robot was originally going to be called “Freedom Fighter Gunboy” during its 1979 development at the animation studio Sunrise. Directed by Yoshiyuki Tomino, its debut TV series established the “real robot” subgenre of mecha anime, favoring mass-produced military hardware over a single invincible hero machine. A moving, 18-meter, 25-ton statue of this franchise’s original robot stood in Yokohama from 2020 until 2024. It was then dismantled for display, arm raised to the sky, at the 2025 World Expo in Osaka. A similar giant statue has also stood on the artificial island of Odaiba, including a temporary model built for the franchise’s 30th anniversary in 2009. Its giant humanoid “mobile suits” are piloted in interstellar wars, and its toy model kits are nicknamed “Gunpla”. For 10 points, name this influential mecha anime and toy franchise that debuted in Japan in 1979.

Since 1973, this intersection has let pedestrians cross diagonally from every corner at once when its lights change, instead of only in an L-shaped pattern. It has been described as the world’s busiest pedestrian crossing, with estimates of up to three thousand people crossing during a single green-light cycle. Sofia Coppola filmed here repeatedly for her 2003 film “Lost in Translation,” including a rain-soaked scene where Scarlett Johansson’s character walks through a sea of translucent umbrellas. It sits outside a train station plaza that also holds a bronze statue of a famously loyal dog, a popular meeting spot for visitors. Overlooked by giant video screens and a busy Starbucks with a bird’s-eye view, it is often compared to New York’s Times Square. For 10 points, name this famously chaotic Tokyo pedestrian crossing.

During this event, Kenjaku — secretly inhabiting the body of sorcerer Suguru Geto — traps Satoru Gojo inside the “Prison Realm” cursed object. That seals away the world’s strongest sorcerer for the next nineteen days. It unfolds on Halloween night of 2018, when a curtain-like barrier drops over a Tokyo entertainment district. That barrier forces student and professional sorcerers into a series of increasingly desperate battles against special-grade curses. Adapting this arc, the second season of “Jujutsu Kaisen” aired in 2023 to a wave of viral reaction videos, as fans watched beloved characters suffer devastating losses in real time. It takes its name from the same crowded shopping and nightlife district as a famous scramble crossing located just blocks from where its worst battles take place. For 10 points, name this Halloween 2018 attack in “Jujutsu Kaisen,” in which Gojo Satoru gets trapped inside a small box.

According to the University of Tokyo, this dog likely waited for his owner at their campus gate during his owner’s lifetime, not at the station most depictions show. His owner, agriculture professor Hidesaburō Ueno, died of a cerebral hemorrhage in May 1925. The dog then began returning each evening to that station to wait, for nearly ten more years until his own death. He was named for the character meaning “eight,” reportedly because his forelegs formed that shape when he stood as a puppy. He personally attended the unveiling of his own bronze statue outside that station in April 1934, about a year before he died. His preserved body has been on permanent display at Tokyo’s National Museum of Nature and Science since shortly after his 1935 death. For 10 points, name this Akita dog famed for his loyalty to a Tokyo professor.

This catchphrase is delivered by Kenshiro, protagonist of the 1983 manga and anime Hokuto no Ken, immediately after he strikes an enemy's secret pressure points using his family's assassination martial art. The stricken opponent notices nothing at first, until moments later, when their body suddenly explodes or crumples apart, prompting a bewildered cry of "NANI?!" A wave of remix videos setting other footage to this line's audio, timed for a shocking beat-drop payoff, went viral on YouTube in the summer of 2017. Combined with a still of its speaker pointing straight at the viewer, it also became a stock reaction image for online arguments. For 10 points, name this Japanese catchphrase, uttered by Kenshiro instants before a fatally struck enemy's body gives out, that became one of anime's most quoted lines online.
answer: Omae wa mou shindeiru [or Omae wa mou shinderu or You are already dead; prompt on NANI]

question: A single-serving Tumblr blog titled "Has Senpai Noticed Me Yet?" launched on 8 August 2012, cataloguing the anime trope of an underclassman pining for an oblivious upperclassman crush. In Japanese schools, the honorific for that older student is the word this phrase's second half comes from. The joke spread through image macros and fan-run ask blogs before a 2014 compilation video by YouTuber PewDiePie carried it to a much wider audience. Today, fans use its imperative form to jokingly beg a celebrity they admire for a reply or acknowledgment on social media. For 10 points, give this three-word plea for an admired upperclassman's attention, a phrase now used broadly online to ask for anyone's recognition.

In the 1980s, Japanese speakers adopted this loanword, pronounced according to their language's syllable structure, as a more neutral alternative to the traditional word "kanai," which carried homemaker connotations. Its current internet sense took off after it was used in a scene of the early-2000s slice-of-life anime Azumanga Daioh. From anime fandom, it spread to describe any fictional character toward whom a fan feels romantic or sexual attraction, alongside a coined male-equivalent term. Psychologists studying the phenomenon describe the attachment some fans form to it as a form of parasocial relationship. For 10 points, give this Japanese-derived slang term, borrowed from and pronounced like an English word for a spouse, for a fan's ideal fictional love interest.

In the original Japanese dialogue and Akira Toriyama's manga, the relevant figure in this line is 8,000; English dub voice actor Brian Drummond changed the number to better match the character's on-screen mouth flaps. The character speaking it, the Saiyan prince Vegeta, gasps this line upon reading a rival's power level on his scouter, right before the device explodes. On 17 October 2006, YouTuber Weston "Kajetokun" Durant uploaded a YouTube Poop mocking the line's awkward English phrasing as an inside joke for friends. Funimation's later re-dub, with Christopher Sabat voicing Vegeta, kept the altered number rather than correcting it. For 10 points, give this exclamatory catchphrase from Dragon Ball Z, now used online as a jokingly hyperbolic way to describe an enormous, uncountable quantity of anything.
answer: it's over 9000 [or it's over nine thousand; or “Over 9000”; or “Over nine thousand”; or “It is over 9000”; or “It is over nine thousand”]

question: Fans coined this figure's nickname on the Reddit community r/manga around 2015, after noticing an absurdly common plot device recurring across dozens of unrelated series, including the manga Fuuka. Its cutesy honorific suffix, typically reserved for young men or those of lower social status, is applied ironically to a machine rather than a person. The joke personifies every such vehicular accident across the isekai genre as a single, sentient entity with one dedicated mission: flattening protagonists so they can be reborn in a fantasy world. Fan art and memes depict it with a mischievous grin, cheerfully closing in on an unsuspecting victim about to cross the street. For 10 points, name this internet nickname for the recurring, personified road vehicle that kills and reincarnates isekai protagonists.

This wagashi confection is traditionally threaded three to five balls at a time onto a skewer. One glazed variety, coated in a sweet soy-based sauce, is said to trace back to a teahouse in Kyoto's Shimogamo neighborhood. A pink-white-green variety associated with cherry-blossom viewing is traditionally said to have debuted at a lavish 1598 viewing party thrown by the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi. A different variety, stacked in a pyramid, is offered to the moon during the autumn viewing festival tsukimi. Made from glutinous rice flour rolled into small round balls, it comes in dozens of regional and seasonal varieties across Japan. For 10 points, name this skewered Japanese rice dumpling, whose mitarashi variety is glazed in sweet soy sauce.

In the Yakuza video game series, protagonist Kiryu Kazuma is frequently shown ordering this dish at restaurants, cementing its association with the franchise's fandom. Series creator Toshihiro Nagoshi once used eating it as a shorthand jab for being an uncool, introverted gamer, a remark that sparked backlash and cemented the dish's use as an internet insult for the same stereotype. Its short slang nickname blends abbreviated forms of its two main components. The base dish beneath the modification is a simple bowl of rice topped with simmered beef and onion in a sweetened soy-based sauce. For 10 points, name this variation on a Japanese beef-and-rice bowl, topped with a melted dairy addition, that became internet slang for an uncool otaku stereotype.

Psychiatrist Tamaki Saito introduced this term to wider clinical attention in a bestselling 1998 book, tracing its roots back to a 1970s phenomenon of Japanese students refusing to attend school. Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare has described it as a "psycho-sociological phenomenon" rather than a single diagnosable disease. Cases surged in Japan during the economic downturn of the 1990s, sometimes nicknamed that decade's "ice age," which blocked many young people from reaching their goals. Diagnostic criteria generally require a marked, continuous withdrawal into a single room of the family home for at least six months. Government estimates now put the number of affected individuals in Japan above one million. For 10 points, give this Japanese term for prolonged, extreme social withdrawal, most often affecting young adults who confine themselves to their bedrooms.

Grammatically, this phrase combines the te-form of a verb meaning "to stop" with a polite imperative ending typically translated "please." Despite representing an entirely ordinary, non-sexual request in standard Japanese conversation, English-language internet culture has overwhelmingly reinterpreted it through the lens of adult anime and ecchi fan content. A popular variant adds a word for "older brother" to the end, tied to anime scenes of playful sibling teasing. The phrase has spawned viral remixes set to EDM drops and heavy metal covers, alongside its use as stock audio in thirst-trap and gaming clips on TikTok. For 10 points, give this Japanese phrase literally translating to "please stop," now an internet-meme shorthand associated with anime characters begging for mercy.

A Japanese proverb built around this food's name holds that a person values substance over appearance, preferring it to admiring cherry blossoms at a picnic. A 1992-2003 shoujo manga punningly retitled that proverb by swapping this food's name for a homophonous word meaning "boys," birthing a title usually translated as Boys Over Flowers. In the folktale of the Peach Boy, a version made from millet is handed out to recruit a talking dog, monkey and pheasant as traveling companions. A 1999 novelty song about a family of three of this food, created for an NHK preschool program, became the best-selling single in Japan that year. For 10 points, name this skewered Japanese dumpling.

Of mixed Japanese and French-Canadian ancestry, this performer leveraged her distinctive Eurasian features to stand out after entering Japan's adult video industry in 2005. She retired from that industry in 2009 after appearing in more than one hundred titles, then rebuilt a mainstream career largely in Southeast Asia rather than her home country, sidestepping the stigma that still followed her there. In 2015 she starred opposite Cesar Montano and Robin Padilla in the horror film Nilalang, entered in that year's Metro Manila Film Festival. More recently, she joined the cast of the GMA-7 historical drama Pulang Araw. For 10 points, name this former Japanese AV idol turned Philippine mainstream actress.

Tea master Murata Juko is generally credited as the originator of this aesthetic philosophy, which reached its most influential form under his eventual successor Sen no Rikyu in the 16th century. Rikyu's stripped-down style of tea ceremony rejected expensive, ornate Chinese ceramics in favor of humble, locally made pottery, reframing the gathering as a space of equality rather than displayed wealth. It emerged from Zen Buddhist teaching during the Muromachi period, and its two component terms individually connote rustic, natural simplicity and the beauty that comes with age and wear. For 10 points, give this compound Japanese aesthetic philosophy that finds beauty in imperfection and transience.

This word's two characters literally mean "outside" and "person," distinguishing it from a longer, more official four-character term meaning "outside-country-person" that refers strictly to non-citizens regardless of appearance. Its earliest written appearance is traced to the 13th-century war epic The Tale of the Heike. Usage of the shorter term surged after World War II, during the Allied Occupation, when it was applied especially to non-Asian, visibly foreign-looking residents. Survey research has found a sharp perception gap around the term: a majority of Japanese respondents rate it as neutral, while a much larger majority of non-Japanese respondents consider it derogatory. For 10 points, give this informal, sometimes contentious Japanese word for a foreigner, contrasted with the more neutral "gaikokujin."

In standard Japanese, this reduplicated word most commonly serves as a childish nursery term for the penis, roughly equivalent to English "pee-pee" or "wee-wee." Confusingly, the same sequence of sounds is also used for a trained dog's begging trick, for hopping on one leg, and for the ringing of a bell or the whistle of a boiling kettle. Sports commentators also use it to describe a lopsided, one-sided victory. In the Aichi Prefecture dialect, however, the same word instead means "scalding hot," completely unrelated to its meaning everywhere else in Japan. For 10 points, give this Japanese reduplicated word, a childish term for male genitalia elsewhere but a synonym for extreme heat in Aichi.

By the Heian period, a kelp-based version of this stock had become indispensable to shojin ryori, the vegetarian cuisine of Buddhist temples. In 1908, Tokyo Imperial University professor Ikeda Kikunae extracted glutamic acid from the kelp used in it and coined the term umami for the taste he'd identified. Five years later, his student Kodama Shintaro found a second flavor compound, inosinic acid, in the dried, fermented bonito flakes also used to make it; combining the two compounds produces a taste response roughly eight times stronger than either alone. Cooks typically prepare it by gently heating kelp and bonito flakes rather than boiling them, to preserve their delicate flavor. For 10 points, name this savory Japanese soup stock, foundational to dishes like miso soup.

This word derives from an older phrase combining terms for "face" and "glowing" or "flushing," originally describing someone blushing. Sanrio designer Yuko Shimizu drew on the aesthetic movement built around this word when she created a white, bow-wearing cat character in 1974, whose name nodded to a feline in Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass before "Hello" was added in front of it. That character's 1975 debut and especially her 1983 launch in the United States helped turn the aesthetic global. For 10 points, give this Japanese word, commonly translated "cute," that names both an adjective and a broader aesthetic movement embracing childlike charm.

This rail system's name literally translates to "new trunk line." Its first route, connecting Tokyo and Osaka, began construction in 1959 across 515 kilometers of difficult, mountainous terrain and opened on 1 October 1964, just before that year's Tokyo Olympics. Travel time between the two cities dropped from about six and a half hours to just four. Despite running at speeds exceeding 200 kilometers per hour, its network has recorded zero passenger fatalities from train accidents since that opening. For 10 points, name this Japanese high-speed rail network, nicknamed the bullet train.

This furniture piece traces back to the Muromachi period, when households built a charcoal brazier called an irori into a sunken floor space for both cooking and warmth. During the Edo period, design refinements produced lighter, more portable versions, and the twentieth century saw its heat source replaced by an electric element. A thin base layer called a shitagake and a thick overlying blanket called a kotatsu-gake work together to trap the rising warm air around people's lower bodies. It offers efficient localized heating especially valuable in traditional Japanese homes, which historically lacked central heating. For 10 points, name this low, blanket-draped Japanese table with a built-in heat source, a cozy gathering spot in winter.

The earliest recorded use of this term appears in a 12th-century Japanese medical scroll describing a real intersex condition rather than any fictional trope. In the 17th century, a related word described male kabuki actors celebrated for convincingly playing both male and female roles. Doujinshi artist Toshiki Yui helped codify its modern visual conventions during the 1980s and 1990s self-published manga scene. Its two Japanese root words literally translate to "two" and "form" or "figure." For 10 points, give this Japanese-derived term for a hentai genre depicting fictional characters possessing both male and female genitalia.

This word's two-character kanji compound literally combines terms for "change to another state" and "condition," originally serving as a biological term for morphological change before Meiji-era psychology repurposed it to describe abnormal sexual desire. In its home country, the word still carries that older clinical sense and refers broadly to any bizarre or perverse sexual conduct, not to any specific artistic medium. English speakers detached the word from that original meaning during the 1990s, narrowing it into a catch-all label for one specific type of adult animation and comics. For 10 points, give this Japanese loanword, used in the West as a genre label for pornographic anime and manga.

This expression's name combines an onomatopoeia for panting or moaning with the Japanese word for "face." Its exaggerated visual conventions, including rolled-back or crossed eyes, a lolling tongue and drool, first appeared in erotic Japanese art circles during the 1960s, though the term for it wasn't used in a commercial manga until Hiromitsu Takeda's 2008 work "I Love Scraper." A 2015 illustration by the artist Hirame went viral and soon appeared on mainstream Western clothing, prompting several American anime conventions to ban the resulting apparel from their premises starting in 2020. For 10 points, give this Japanese term for an exaggerated facial expression of intense pleasure, common in hentai artwork.

Cure Maid Café, which opened in Akihabara in March 2001, is generally credited as the first permanent example of this business concept, and it still operates today with a Victorian-styled atmosphere and Saturday live music as a certified tea restaurant. Staff dressed in costume treat customers as a returning master or mistress arriving home, rather than as ordinary patrons of a commercial establishment. The concept boomed across Akihabara through the early 2000s before declining sharply alongside the district's broader fall from otaku prominence, leaving fewer than thirty such establishments in the neighborhood by 2026. For 10 points, name this style of themed Japanese café, staffed by costumed servers.

Founded by the Seibu Retailing Group, this chain opened its first store in Sayama, Saitama Prefecture, in September 1973. It has been a subsidiary of the trading conglomerate ITOCHU Corporation since 2009. Now Japan's second-largest convenience store chain by store count, it has expanded to roughly 25,000 locations across Japan, Taiwan, China, the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia. Its blue-green-and-white striped logo marks thousands of storefronts across the country. For 10 points, name this Japanese convenience store chain.

Creator Kole Sims, who has Filipino-Japanese heritage, built this TikTok account around confessional street interviews conducted in the Shibuya district. Subjects, sometimes caught a little drunk on a night out, are approached with a camera and asked surprisingly personal questions, and their unfiltered, rambling answers became the account's signature. Individual clips and recurring interview subjects have separately spun off into their own meme formats among Gen Z audiences. The account grew past one million followers largely on the strength of this raw, chaotic honesty. For 10 points, name this viral street-interview TikTok account named for its creator and the Japanese capital where it films.

This phrase began as the opening words of a January 2013 4chan /jp/ copypasta that rewrote the aggressive "Navy Seal Copypasta" monologue by swapping in Japanese vocabulary wherever the English original sat, replacing words like "I" and "you" with watashi and anata. A viral dramatic YouTube reading helped the bilingual rant spread to Reddit and Urban Dictionary. Over time, its first three words broke off from the rest of the copypasta to become a standalone slang exclamation in their own right. For 10 points, give this ironic, anime-accented exclamation of disbelief, combining the Japanese word for "what" with a common English expletive.
answer: Nani the fuck [or Nani da fuck; prompt on nani]

question: This game's mechanical ancestor is a 1920s American children's pastime called Corinthian Bagatelle, which reached Nagoya and was adapted into an adult pursuit there. Masamura Takeuchi is generally credited as the figure who turned it into its modern form, and the first commercial parlor for it opened in Nagoya in 1948, the same year Japan's Act on Control and Improvement of Amusement Business formally recognized the industry. Japanese law does not classify it as gambling, because winners exchange their prizes for cash only at a separate, technically unaffiliated shop away from the parlor floor, rather than for money on-site. For 10 points, name this wildly popular Japanese arcade game, played by launching small steel balls into a vertical pinball-like machine.

Its Japanese name combines words for "embrace" and "pillow." Originally just an ordinary long pillow used for extra sleep support, its design shifted in the 1990s as the anime and manga industry began printing character artwork onto its covers. The company Cospa was among the producers releasing covers depicting reclining bishoujo and bishonen characters as the product intertwined with otaku culture in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Fans use it both as a comfort object and as a way to express devotion to a favorite fictional character. For 10 points, name this oversized Japanese pillow, often printed with an anime character design and embraced by devoted fans as a stand-in romantic partner.

According to Buddhist legend, this dance began when the disciple Mokuren, overjoyed after freeing his deceased mother's spirit from the Realm of Hungry Ghosts by following the Buddha's instructions to make offerings to monks, danced for joy. That religious nenbutsu ceremony evolved over time into public folk entertainment, with the tradition said to have taken its modern form as public entertainment in the late Muromachi period. Obon, the broader festival it belongs to, has been celebrated in Japan for more than five hundred years to welcome home the spirits of deceased ancestors for a brief visit. For 10 points, name this traditional Japanese folk dance performed during the Obon festival.

In everyday Japanese, this noun refers to a temporary feeling or sensation brought on by some outside stimulus, distinct from more lasting emotional states. Paired with an adjective meaning "good," it forms a common two-word phrase used to say something feels pleasant, from a cool breeze to a satisfying stretch. Online, however, international audiences encountered that same two-word phrase almost exclusively through hentai and adult-video dialogue, where characters moan it to express physical pleasure during sex scenes. That narrow exposure has left many English-speaking internet users associating the base word almost entirely with pornography, despite its mundane everyday use in Japan. For 10 points, give this common Japanese word for "feeling," whose paired phrase with "ii" became internet-famous through adult anime.

A Japanese physician coined the clinical term for this phenomenon in 1982, though its first reported case is usually traced back to 1969, when a 29-year-old newspaper shipping-department worker died of a stroke. By the 1990s, an advocacy group tracking it estimated roughly ten thousand annual victims in Japan. The advertising agency Dentsu became notorious for it after 24-year-old employee Ichiro Oshima's 1991 suicide, following a month with 147 hours of overtime, led his family to a Japanese Supreme Court victory. A second Dentsu case, the 2015 suicide of 24-year-old Matsuri Takahashi after 105 overtime hours in a month, reignited public pressure for a legal cap on overtime hours. For 10 points, give this Japanese term for death caused by overwork.

This word's noun form derives from a verb combining an intensifying prefix with another verb meaning "to pour" or "shower," literally describing a forceful splash. In Japan, it most commonly appears in food names for cold noodles served with hot broth poured directly over them, as in dishes ending in udon or soba. Because the everyday splashing sense predates its other associations, most Japanese speakers still react to hearing the food term with simple hunger rather than any other reaction. In 2021, the noodle chain Marugame Udon renamed one of its dishes for the American market specifically to avoid this word, whose secondary meaning in English differs sharply from its primary Japanese sense. For 10 points, give this Japanese word, primarily meaning "splash" or "pour," that also names a genre of pornography.

This compound insult combines a vulgar word for excrement with a term originally borrowed from Buddhist cosmology for a hungry ghost, later broadened in everyday speech to mean simply "brat" or "kid." Literally translating to something like "damn brat," it can be lobbed as a genuine insult or used affectionately between close friends depending on tone. In anime, being addressed with this word has become such a reliable genre signal that hearing it practically announces a character will turn out headstrong, disrespectful, or too proud to back down. For 10 points, give this Japanese slang term of abuse for a bratty, unruly child.

Coined at the tail end of the Sengoku period as a formal way for one samurai to address a letter to another, this pronoun began as a polite, honorific way to refer to members of samurai households. It entered everyday spoken use during the Edo period, and its meaning gradually flattened alongside Japanese society itself after the Meiji Restoration's rapid modernization. By the early twentieth century it had flipped entirely, becoming a hostile term barked by military officers at subordinates; one competing theory traces that shift instead to prostitutes using it to address customers. For 10 points, give this now-derogatory Japanese second-person pronoun, equivalent to "you scum" and a common confrontational insult in anime dialogue right before a fight.

This portmanteau term entered Japanese usage in the 1970s, borrowed from a 1966 English-language book title that itself referenced a controversial 1955 novel. Legal scholars have since written extensively about how Japan's 1999 child pornography statute criminalized the production and distribution of real child sexual abuse material, while a 2014 amendment that criminalized simple possession of such material explicitly carved out an exemption for fictional, drawn depictions, keeping them legal to possess. That carve-out has drawn sustained international criticism and calls for Japan to bring its law into compliance with international obligations addressing fictional depictions of this kind. Scholars trace the underlying Japanese cultural concept less to the American novel that inspired its name than to an older, more sentimental idealization of girlhood culture dating back to the Meiji period. For 10 points, give this Japanese portmanteau term for an attraction to, or fictional genre depicting, underage-appearing characters, contracted from an English phrase describing an adult attraction to young girls.

This rhetorical question originated on 4chan's /a/ board in 2009, mocking fans' tendency to spot connections to a certain manga in completely unrelated images, from casual poses to random kanji. That manga, created by Hirohiko Araki starting in 1987, became one of the longest-running successful series in its medium and influenced countless later works, giving the joke an almost inexhaustible supply of material. In September 2016, YouTube creator Mundano XXXIII uploaded a video dubbing the manga's own music over an unrelated Pokemon gameplay clip, helping the joke reach critical mass across platforms by that November. For 10 points, give this ironic exclamation, aimed at fans who find allusions to Hirohiko Araki's bizarre manga series everywhere they look.
answer: Is that a JoJo reference [or Is this a JoJo reference; or “JoJo reference”; or “Is this a JoJos reference”; or “Is that a JoJos reference”]

question: No single definitive origin story exists for this lucky charm, though the most widely accepted legend centers on Gotokuji Temple in Tokyo's Setagaya ward. In the early 17th century, a temple cat is said to have beckoned the feudal lord Ii Naotaka inside for shelter from a sudden thunderstorm. In gratitude, Naotaka became the temple's patron, and it was later renamed using characters from his posthumous Buddhist name. After the cat's death, priests built a hall there now filled with thousands of small white cat statues, in gratitude for the prosperity it brought the temple. For 10 points, name this raised-paw Japanese cat figurine, believed to invite good fortune and customers into a shop or home.

Despite widespread belief, this line was never actually spoken in the original Japanese anime, any of its dubs, or the source manga, making it a kind of collective false memory. Fans nonetheless attribute it to the villain Frieza, imagined taunting his stunned opponents right after unveiling merely his second or third of several transformations. One of the earliest traceable posts of the phrase as a stand-alone meme, captioned under a photo of an unrelated sculpture, appeared on FunnyJunk on 24 September 2011. It grew steadily through the early 2010s within otaku internet communities as a stock phrase for something surprisingly not yet at its peak. For 10 points, give this popularly misremembered Dragon Ball Z catchphrase, in which a villain boasts of further transformations still to come.
answer: This isn't even my final form [or “You fool, this isn't even my final form”; or “This is not even my final form”]

question: This food-preference meme often pairs its central character’s favorite snack with her aversion to carrots, creating a contrast between two foods. The child at the center of the joke can read minds, which lets her discover secrets that her adoptive parents hide. Her father Loid is a spy and her mother Yor is an assassin, although the household presents itself as an ordinary family. Fans of Spy x Family turn this young Forger’s enthusiasm for a particular crunchy legume into captions and other jokes. For 10 points, give this short meme declaration naming the telepathic girl and the food she especially enjoys as a snack.

The initial official English release of a panel associated with this meme used a single negative word before a correction restored its familiar wording. That panel appears in chapter 221 of Gege Akutami’s manga and echoes an earlier exchange from the third chapter. Edits replace the pictured character or redraw the panel, often making the speaker’s confidence look increasingly implausible or comically misplaced. Satoru Gojo delivers the reply in Jujutsu Kaisen when discussing a possible confrontation with Sukuna and dismissing the prospect of defeat. For 10 points, give this confident response predicting victory, beginning with a casual alternative to the word “no”.

The speaker of this declaration apologizes to Riko Amanai while acknowledging that his current euphoric feeling has displaced his grief. He has recovered from a seemingly fatal encounter by learning to use a reverse cursed technique to heal himself. During his rematch with Toji Fushiguro, this sorcerer floats above his opponent before demonstrating an attack called Hollow Purple. The line spoken by Satoru Gojo echoes a saying associated with the Buddha and expresses an overwhelming sense of personal supremacy. For 10 points, give this Jujutsu Kaisen declaration in which Gojo claims a uniquely exalted status across both celestial and terrestrial realms.
answer: “Throughout heaven and earth, I alone am the honored one” [or “I alone am the honored one”; or “I alone am the honoured one”; or “Throughout heaven and earth I alone am the honoured one”; or “The honored one”; or “The honoured one”; or “I am the honored one”; or “I am the honoured one”]

question: The recipient of this compliment imagines his companions Hanami and Dagon near the end of a battle he cannot survive. That recipient had helped awaken his eventual opponent by feeding cursed fingers to Yuji, hoping to recruit the being within him. Hearing his abilities acknowledged causes the defeated cursed spirit to shed tears, despite previously being treated dismissively by Satoru Gojo. Sukuna delivers this rare praise to Jogo, a volcano-headed opponent whose attacks include fiery techniques and a massive meteor. For 10 points, give this Jujutsu Kaisen line that encourages the defeated fighter to retain his dignity and recognizes his formidable ability.
answer: “Stand proud, you’re strong” [or “Stand proud you are strong”; or “Stand proud”]

question: An official promotional upload repeated the sequence associated with this chant for a full hour before the corresponding television anime premiered. Posted in May 2024, that loop shows Torako dancing while facing a deer, creating an unusually persistent musical advertisement. Fans recreated the movement with other characters, turning the repeated snippet into a dance meme well beyond the original promotional video. The syllables form the Japanese title of the series known in English as My Deer Friend Nokotan and appear in its opening music. For 10 points, identify this deer-themed dance meme by its repeated Japanese chant or the title of the opening song that supplies it.
answer: “Shikanoko nokonoko koshitantan” [or “Shikanoko nokonoko koshi tantan”; or “Shikanokonokonokokoshitantan”; or “Shikairo Days”; or “Shikairo Days Dance”; or “Shikanoko”]

question: The character associated with this greeting is designated laboratory member number 002 and spends some of her spare time making cosplay outfits. She is a childhood friend of Rintaro Okabe, whose attempts to alter events place her at the center of repeated crises. Using the nickname Mayushii for herself, she delivers the sound in a cheerful, singsong manner when introducing herself or arriving. This greeting belongs to Mayuri Shiina in Steins;Gate, providing a lighthearted contrast to the series’ increasingly dangerous experiments with time. For 10 points, imitate or name this brief melodic greeting, usually romanized with an opening “tu” and an extended final vowel.

The character who uses this expression gives himself the theatrical alias Hououin Kyouma, presenting his activities as those of a mad scientist. He claims to face a mysterious Organization, mixing grandiose conspiratorial language with the everyday life of his small laboratory. His Reading Steiner ability lets him remember events after changes to the timeline, making him crucial to the story’s time-travel experiments. Rintaro Okabe repeatedly utters this peculiar three-word catchphrase in Steins;Gate, even though the expression itself has no established meaning. For 10 points, give this cryptic phrase associated with Okabe, whose final word is often romanized with either an initial K or C.

An early documented appearance of this meme was on the Tanasinn wiki in 2007, alongside a screenshot featuring Light Yagami. A translator’s note at the top of the image explains a Japanese term that the subtitle has unnecessarily left untranslated. The caption became a way to mock fan translations that preserve Japanese vocabulary even when a straightforward English equivalent exists. Its final word refers to an intended course of action, so the explanatory annotation undermines the apparent need to retain that foreign term in the first place. For 10 points, give this Death Note subtitle meme expressing that events have unfolded as intended, in its mixed-language wording or its English equivalent.
answer: “Just according to keikaku” [or “All according to keikaku”; or “Keikaku”; or “Just as planned”; or “Just according to plan”; or “All according to plan”]

question: This line’s visual presentation includes slow motion and sparkling fragments, giving an everyday action an extravagantly dramatic treatment on screen. YouTube Poop remixes of the scene appeared in 2007, helping turn its delivery into a recurring joke among online viewers. The original scene appears in “Glare”, the eighth episode of an anime about a notebook that can cause a person’s death. Light Yagami delivers this declaration in Death Note, announcing an ordinary snack-related action with the intensity of a decisive strategic maneuver. For 10 points, give this melodramatic line in which Kira declares his intention to consume a single thin, crispy fried slice.
answer: “I’ll take a potato chip and eat it” [or “I will take a potato chip and eat it”; or “Potato chip”]

question: Edits of this viral boast have included Monika from Doki Doki Literature Club, placing an unrelated fictional character into the joke. Other remixes inserted the clip into scenes from Revenge of the Sith, recasting its speaker as an unexpectedly confident combatant. The original live-action video spread through Twitter and YouTube in July 2017 and ends with the child’s emphatic battle cry. The speaker announces two very different sources of support before shouting, combining religious backing with enthusiasm for Japanese animated entertainment. For 10 points, name this meme boast claiming that both a divine being and a favorite animation medium are supporting the speaker.
answer: “The power of God and anime” [or “I have the power of God and anime on my side”; or “God and anime”]

question: Context for this notorious subtitle involves Avalon, an implanted magical sheath responsible for its speaker’s unusually effective ability to recover from injuries. Kiritsugu Emiya placed that object inside the speaker, explaining why a seemingly obvious observation about mortality had a less ordinary context. Removed from that context, the sentence circulated alongside reaction jokes expressing disbelief that such an obvious statement needed to be spoken. Shirou Emiya delivers the line in Studio Deen’s 2006 adaptation of Fate/stay night, where supernatural survival complicates ordinary expectations. For 10 points, give this tautological anime quote asserting that a fatal attack normally results in the victim’s death.
answer: “People die if they are killed” [or “People die when they are killed”]

question: This nickname praises a television adaptation directed by Takahiro Miura, whose first season aired in 2014 and whose second followed in 2015. The production adapts a route from a Type-Moon visual novel, following Shirou Emiya’s involvement in the fifth Holy Grail War. Fans use the phrase to praise ufotable’s lavish animation, especially the visual spectacle accompanying battles between mages and summoned heroes. The joke alters the subtitle of this Fate/stay night adaptation by substituting a term for financial resources for a word describing weapons. For 10 points, give this three-word anime nickname suggesting that the studio had no spending ceiling when producing its impressive action scenes.

A line spoken by Quentin Quire in an X-Men comic has been interpreted as a reference to this familiar anime meme. The command is associated with a character whose clasped hands and stern expression have inspired their own widely imitated pose. That character, Gendo Ikari, leads NERV and maintains a troubled relationship with the teenage son whom he summons to pilot Unit 01. Fans of Neon Genesis Evangelion use this impatient order as a shorthand for a father’s demand that his reluctant child become a pilot. For 10 points, give this meme instruction telling the younger Ikari to enter the giant machine he is expected to control.
answer: “Get in the robot, Shinji” [or “Get in the robot”]

question: The episode ending with this repeated word carries the alternate English title “Take Care of Yourself” and focuses on Instrumentality. Earlier in that episode, an alternate reality presents familiar characters as ordinary students and family members in a domestic-comedy setting. Shinji comes to recognize that he can change how he understands himself, culminating in a scene surrounded by familiar faces. The cast applauds him while repeating this expression at the end of the original Neon Genesis Evangelion television series. For 10 points, give this celebratory word, or its Japanese equivalent, that the characters address to Shinji during the famous finale.

This Japanese command appears beneath a red-tinted bird in a reaction image used to express disapproval or disagreement. Despite that image’s common name, the photographed bird is a grackle, and its captioned version circulated on Imgur in 2017. Grammatically, this expression uses the plain imperative form of a verb meaning to cease an activity or to quit. The final syllable of this conjugated command is “ro”, giving learners a way to distinguish it from softer requests. For 10 points, give this forceful Japanese command meaning “stop it”, or name the disapproving bird meme that uses it as a caption.
answer: “Yamero” [or “Crow of Judgement”; or “Crow of Judgment”; or “Yamero Crow”]

question: Flash animations drew on a 1998 Capcom fighting game to spread this shouted phrase, often combining it with exaggerated attack sequences. The associated visual effect changes the surrounding colors before movement freezes, allowing the attacker to act while opponents remain motionless. Knives and a steamroller feature among attacks linked with the character who shouts this phrase during his confrontation with Jotaro. Dio uses it to invoke his time-stopping Stand in JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure, and fans reproduce the Japanese pronunciation for comic emphasis. For 10 points, give this shouted Stand name, whose English translation names the entire planet and whose pronunciation became an internet catchphrase.

The music associated with this video meme comes from a Yes recording included on the progressive-rock band’s 1971 album Fragile. The tune served as an ending theme during the anime adaptations of Phantom Blood and Battle Tendency, linking it with cliffhangers. Online edits spread through Vine and YouTube, timing the musical buildup to an ordinary scene about to go spectacularly wrong. A freeze-frame and a prominent arrow interrupt the action before its outcome, imitating an ending device from JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure. For 10 points, name this cliffhanger meme by its arrow’s three-word caption, or identify the Yes song used to build suspense before the freeze-frame.

This reveal comes from an early Phantom Blood encounter and appears in the first episode of the 2012 television adaptation. Its speaker targets Erina Pendleton in an attempt to humiliate Jonathan Joestar, turning a romantic expectation into an unwanted surprise. The scene follows a stolen kiss, after which the antagonist triumphantly identifies himself as the person responsible for the encounter. Online variations use the declaration as a bait-and-switch punchline, replacing something expected with the grinning villain from JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure. For 10 points, give this villain’s Japanese self-reveal, or its familiar English rendering, announcing that he was the unexpected culprit.
answer: “Kono Dio da” [or “It was me Dio”; or “But it was me Dio”]

question: Professional wrestler Marcellus Black adopted this catchphrase in connection with a running-knee attack, taking an idol joke into another performance setting. The original anime scene appears in a fifth episode from 2013, when a character demonstrates how a proper idol should behave. Fans remixed the repeated syllables into videos and musical edits, often preserving the speaker’s exaggeratedly cheerful delivery and hand gestures. The performer is Yazawa, a school idol from the Love Live franchise who uses the routine as her distinctive introduction. For 10 points, give this singsong idol catchphrase, built around a repeated two-syllable name and usually accompanied by a deliberately adorable pose.
answer: “Nico Nico Nii” [or “Nico Nico Ni”; or “NicoNicoNii”; or “Niko Niko Nii”]
